blocks.text: Applications such as Notepad and Microsoft Word use a stack for undo. Each action, such as typing or deleting text, is pushed onto a stack. Pressing undo pops the most recent action and reverses it; pressing again reverses the one before. If you typed 'Hello' and then 'World', undo removes 'World' first and then 'Hello'.

blocks.title: Python code (each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
class Stack:
....def __init__(self):
........self.items = []
....def push(self, item):
........self.items.append(item)
....def pop(self):
........return self.items.pop()
....def peek(self):
........return self.items[-1]

plates = Stack()
for plate in ["Plate 1", "Plate 2", "Plate 3"]:
....plates.push(plate)
....print(plates.items)
print("Removed:", plates.pop(), "Stack:", plates.items)
print("Top plate:", plates.peek())    # Plate 2

blocks.prompt: Class activity: write a Stack class for plates in a restaurant kitchen with push, pop and peek; push Plate 1, 2, 3, pop one, then peek. What is printed at the end?
blocks.explanation: The code above (not from the book) shows the stack growing to Plate 1, Plate 2, Plate 3; pop removes Plate 3, leaving Plate 1, Plate 2; peek shows Plate 2.

blocks.prompt: Discuss two real-world uses of stacks and how the operations work in them (long question 3).
blocks.explanation: Undo in a text editor: each edit is pushed; undo pops the latest edit and reverses it, so edits are undone newest first. Browser back button: each visited page is pushed; Back pops the current page and shows the one below it. A pile of plates works the same way: new plates go on top and the top plate is taken first.

items: Undo: actions pushed, undo pops the latest; a Stack class needs push, pop and peek.
